primer.title: Shared behaviour, checked at compile time
body: A trait names behaviour; `impl Trait for Type` provides it. A method with a body in the trait is a **default**: an empty `impl` block inherits it, and any impl may override it.
`impl A + B` (or `T: A + B`) in a parameter means the argument's type must implement **both** traits. The check happens where the function is *called*.
Generics are resolved at compile time, not at runtime: `Wrapper<i32>` and `Wrapper<&str>` are two unrelated types. A `Vec` holds exactly one of them.
`.into()` converts to whatever type the context demands, using a `From` impl — e.g. `u8` and `i8` both widen losslessly into `i16`.

options.rationale: Which impl runs depends on the receiver's type. On a `String` it appends text, twice. On a `Vec<String>` it pushes a new element.
The `Vec<String>` impl pushes a new element; it does not call `append_bar` on each string inside.
`append_bar` returns `Self`, so the calls chain: each one appends another `Bar`.

options.text: It does not compile: the trait says `self`, the impls say `mut self`
options.rationale: `mut` on a by-value parameter is a detail of the body, not part of the signature.
`SomeSoftware` overrides the method; `OtherSoftware`'s empty impl inherits the default body from the trait.
An impl that defines the method replaces the default for that type.

options.text: It does not compile: `impl Licensed for OtherSoftware {}` implements nothing
options.rationale: An empty impl is valid when every trait method has a default body.

options.text: It does not compile: `describe` cannot accept two different types
options.rationale: `&impl Licensed` makes `describe` generic. It is compiled once for each type it is called with.

exercises.prompt: Tap the line the compiler rejects.
code: fn both(item: impl SomeTrait + OtherTrait) -> bool {
exercises.rationale: Line 25 passes an `OtherStruct`, which implements `SomeTrait` only. `both` demands `SomeTrait + OtherTrait` (E0277).

lineRationales.19: The signature is valid — it is the contract. The error is reported at the call that fails to meet it.
lineRationales.20: Inside `both`, the bounds guarantee that both methods exist. This line can never be the problem.
lineRationales.17: Implementing just one of the traits is legal. It only means this type cannot be passed to `both`.

exercises.fallbackRationale: That line compiles. Check which traits each struct implements, then look at the calls.

exercises.prompt: This does not compile. What does the compiler object to?

options.text: E0308: `items` is a `Vec<Wrapper<i32>>`, and line 16 pushes a `Wrapper<&str>`
options.rationale: `Wrapper<i32>` and `Wrapper<&str>` are distinct types. Line 15 fixes the element type; a `Vec` holds one type only.
Generics are not dynamic typing. `T` is replaced by one concrete type per value, at compile time.

options.text: E0282: the type of `T` cannot be inferred on lines 12 and 13
options.rationale: It is inferred from each argument: `42` gives `i32`, `"Foo"` gives `&str`.

options.text: E0277: `T` needs a `Display` bound to be printed
options.rationale: Only `items.len()` is printed. `value` is never formatted.
`push` expects an `i16`, so each `.into()` picks `From<u8>` or `From<i8>` for `i16`. Both conversions are lossless.

options.text: It does not compile: a `Vec` cannot hold both `u8` and `i8`
options.rationale: It never does. Each value is converted to `i16` before it is pushed.
That would be reinterpreting the bits of -1 as unsigned. `From` conversions preserve the *value*.

options.text: It does not compile: `.into()` needs an explicit target type
options.rationale: The target is inferred from the context: `numbers` is a `Vec<i16>`.
